addedLines: - augmentor: Implements a single, sharp, well-defined feature or change in an existing codebase with minimal blast radius, staying strictly in line with the codebase's established conventions. Use when you have ONE clearly-scoped addition or modification and want it done surgically. Give it the full spec plus any context you have already gathered; it will fetch whatever else it needs to understand the code. Do NOT use for broad, vague, or multi-feature work, or for anything that would force it to guess at requirements — it will refuse rather than assume. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- bugger: Finds and/or fixes bugs within a defined scope, according to orchestrator/user instructions. Operates in two dimensions. Trigger: either it's told about a specific bug (reproduce → find root cause → address it), or it's asked to scan a part of the code for latent bugs. Action: either propose solutions only (diagnosis + recommended fix, no code changed), or actually implement the fix. The instructions tell it which. When it writes fixes, they are surgical and adhere to the codebase's established standards. Use for debugging and bug-hunting; not for building new features. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- debloater: Reviews a specific piece of code or part of the codebase to remove bloat (dead code, redundancy, needless complexity) and improve logical organization, within a defined scope. Two action modes: IDENTIFY only (report the bloat and improvement opportunities it finds, changing nothing) or CLEAN (actually make the improvements). Under no circumstances does it make changes for their own sake — if nothing genuinely needs changing, it changes nothing and says so. Use for cleanup/tidying/simplification of existing code; not for adding features or fixing bugs. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- doccer: Documents code within a defined boundary — e.g. code an augmentor just wrote, a file/module/directory, or whatever the user points it at. Collects the context it needs, then writes documentation that matches the codebase's established documentation standards and/or the user's instructions (user instructions always win). Use when you want existing code documented without touching the code itself. It will NEVER modify code — not even to fix obvious bugs or errors; it only adds or edits documentation. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- enforcer: Scans code for (1) security issues and vulnerabilities and (2) violations of the codebase's conventions/standards, within a given scope — a specific file, a directory, or a global scan. Two action modes: REPORT only (surface findings to the user/orchestrator, change nothing) or FIX (apply the corrections surgically, conforming to established standards). Use for security review and convention/compliance enforcement. Not for adding features, general bug-hunting, or cleanup/refactoring for its own sake. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- merge-therapist: Resolves merge (or rebase/cherry-pick) conflicts and reports back a highly concise explanation of what it did. Default posture is the most harmonious resolution possible: preserve the intent and functionality of BOTH sides. If the user/orchestrator gives different instructions (prefer one side, drop something, take a specific shape), it follows those instead. Use when a merge/rebase leaves conflicted files, or when you want an in-progress conflict state untangled and explained. Not for doing the merge strategy planning, feature work, or bug-hunting beyond what conflict resolution requires. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, TodoWrite)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- tester: Verifies that ONE specific, already-implemented feature or issue actually behaves the way it is supposed to. Give it (1) what the feature is and (2) what "working" looks like; it exercises the feature — reading code to orient, running curl/CLI/REPL calls, and writing throwaway ad-hoc tests in its own scratch environment — and reports whether the expected behavior holds, with evidence. It does NOT write unit tests into the repo, does NOT modify the codebase, and does NOT review code quality/conventions. Use to confirm a finished change does what it claims; not for building, fixing, or broad regression testing. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, LSP, WebFetch)

20	**When creating AI components, invoke skills using the Skill tool:**
21	
22	- `/create-agent` - new agents
23	- `/create-tool` - new tools
24	- `/create-api` - API clients
25	
26	Skills are defined in `../../.claude/skills/`.
27	
28	## Architecture Principles
29	
30	**Interface Segregation (ISP) — before adding a field/method to a shared base class, mixin, or widely-imported type, ask:**
31	
32	1. **Who actually consumes this?** List the concrete call sites/subclasses. If it's one or two out of many, it doesn't belong on the shared base.
33	2. **Does every consumer need it, or just care about it?** "Might be useful later" or "only some agents use it" is a signal to push it down, not up.
34	3. **Can it be separated?** A field-specific subclass, a small composable mixin, or a standalone parameter object are all preferable to growing a shared base.
35	
36	**Making a field `X | None = None` does not satisfy ISP.** Optionality hides the coupling instead of removing it — every other consumer of the base type still has to know the field exists, decide whether to populate it, and reason about what `None` means for them. The dependency is still there; it's just silent. If most subclasses would leave a field `None` forever, that's a sign it never belonged on the base.
37	
38	**Concrete example — `BaseAgentRequest`** (`projects/ai_agents/src/api/domain/requests/base_agent_request.py`): this is the shared parent for every agent request type (`DefaultAgentRequest`, `ArdoqAssistantAgentRequest`, `ReportInsightAgentRequest`, `CustomAgentRequest`, etc. — see `agent_requests.py`). `web_search_enabled` is agent-specific — it's declared independently on `ArdoqAssistantAgentRequest` and `CodeArdoqAssistantAgentRequest`, *not* hoisted onto the base — that's the pattern to follow. `report_id` on `ReportInsightAgentRequest` and `spec` on `CustomAgentRequest` are further examples of fields that live on the one subclass that needs them.
39	
40	When you catch yourself about to add a new field to `BaseAgentRequest` (or any other shared base type in this codebase): default to adding it on the specific subclass(es) that need it instead. Only promote something to the base after it's genuinely needed by all — or nearly all — consumers, not just "might be handy."
41	
42	This applies beyond `BaseAgentRequest` — the same reasoning applies to any shared base model, tool wrapper config, or widely-imported dataclass. Prefer composition (small, focused types combined via inheritance/mixins or passed alongside) over one growing base that every consumer has to opt in or out of.
43	
44	## Request-ambient state: carry it in the context var
45	
46	Per-request state that many layers need — logger, Ardoq API identity, feature flags, locale, trace id — belongs on the request-scoped `RequestContext`, not in function signatures. Enter it once at the entrypoint with `set_request_context(ctx)` (FastAPI middleware, eval harness, sandbox, test fixture); read it where you use it with `get_request_ctx()`. A missing context raises `NoRequestContextError`, so wiring bugs surface loudly.
47	
48	Keep this for genuinely cross-cutting request state only. Pass business data that one function needs as a normal parameter — the context var is not a place to park arbitrary values.
49	
50	### Segment the context; reach optional groups through a loud accessor
51	
52	Put always-present state directly on `RequestContext` (`logger`, `enabled_features`, `locale`). Group fields that only travel together and only exist on some paths into their own optional sub-context — `ArdoqApiCtx` (`authorization` + `base_url` + `instance_url`, present only when there's a real Ardoq API to call) and `ViewContext` (`ui_commands` + `asset_context`, present only on the UI-command path).
53	
54	Reach an optional group through its accessor so misuse fails at the boundary: check `ctx.has_api`, and call `require_api(ctx)` when you need it — it raises `NoArdoqApiContextError` right there on a headless path, instead of handing back a `None` that explodes several frames later. On paths with no API, leave `api_ctx=None`; represent absence honestly rather than filling in placeholder auth.
55	
56	### Locate each field where it's consumed
57	
58	Group what travels together, and put each field on the type that actually uses it. A good check: if you moved every field on a shared base to where it's consumed, would the base still have fields? If it would empty out, those fields were mislocated — that's the same coupling as threading state through signatures, and the same fix applies: keep state next to its consumer and make absence explicit.
59	
60	## Simplicity
61	
62	**YAGNI / KISS — the same "who needs this, and do they need it now?" reasoning from the ISP section applies one step earlier: before designing an interface at all, not just before adding a field to one.** Build for the concrete case in front of you. Two recurring ways this gets missed:
63	
64	- **Don't add config knobs, feature flags, generic `dict[str, Any]` payloads, or `**kwargs` passthroughs for a hypothetical second use case.** If there's exactly one caller and one concrete need today, give it a concrete, narrow signature. Generality earns its place when a second real caller shows up needing it — not before.
65	- **Don't introduce a new abstract base class, strategy pattern, or plugin registry until there are genuinely 2+ concrete implementations that need it now.** One concrete case gets a plain function or a straight `if`/`match` — not a framework. This is not a ban on abstraction: `pipeline/core/step.py`'s `Step` ABC is a good example of earned abstraction — multiple concrete pipeline implementations depend on it today, so the interface pays for itself. The difference is whether the second consumer already exists, not whether one might exist someday.
66	
67	Two specific instances of this same "keep it simple" reasoning, worth calling out on their own:
68	
69	**Prefer `enum.StrEnum` over ad-hoc string/dict parsing for closed sets of known values — especially in the request layer.**
70	
71	A request field that only ever takes a handful of known string values is a Python `StrEnum`, not a `str`. The tell that this was missed: a field typed loosely (`str`, `str | None`, or `dict[str, Any]`), plus a small cluster of helper functions that each re-parse or re-validate that value (`if value == "x": ...`, a lookup dict keyed by the same strings, a validator re-declaring the allowed values). If you're writing more than one function to interpret the same set of string values, stop and check whether an enum removes the need for most of them — `match`/lookups become exhaustive and type-checked, invalid values are rejected at the pydantic boundary for free, and the valid set is defined in exactly one place instead of scattered across every function that branches on it.
72	
73	Good reference: `ModelId` (`ardoq_ai/config/deployments.py`) — a `StrEnum` used directly as both the on-the-wire request field (`BaseAgentRequest.model`) and the lookup key into `REGISTRY`. One definition, no separate "is this a valid model id" helper, no parallel dict mapping strings to behavior.
74	
75	This is not a blanket rule — free-form user text, genuinely open-ended/extensible values, or data straight from an external API response are not enum candidates just because a `match` statement would look nice. Reach for it specifically when the set of values is small, fixed, and defined by us (request fields, internal modes/categories, discriminators) — not when the value space is inherently open.
76	
77	**Module-level variables belong at module level only if the module-level scope is doing something — shared by multiple functions in the file, imported elsewhere, or expensive enough to want computed once.** A constant declared above a single function and used only inside that function is misleading: it reads as shared/module state, but nothing else in the codebase (or even the file) depends on it being there. Declare it inside the function instead.
78

NOT for exploratory "how does this work" mental-model requests (use mindmap for those), and NOT a substitute for actually writing the code.
- mindmap: Build a high-level, holistic conceptual map of how something in a codebase works — a whole codebase, a feature, a subsystem, a flow, or any specific thing the user points at. Use this when the user wants to *understand how something works* at an intuitive, big-picture level rather than a line-by-line walkthrough or a code edit. Triggers on requests like "explain how X works", "give me a mental model of", "how does this fit together", "map out", "I want to understand the architecture/flow of", "walk me through conceptually", "make sense of this codebase". NOT for making code changes, doing detailed code review, or answering a narrow factual lookup where a one-line answer suffices.
- tune: Extract the user's corrections and preferences from the current conversation and write them into the persistent behavioural instructions (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and the project memory directory). Use when the user says "tune", "update your instructions", "remember how I want you to work", "apply my feedback to your behaviour", or after a conversation where they corrected style, process, or output format. NOT for saving factual/project knowledge (that is ordinary memory) and NOT for one-off instructions that apply only to the current task.
- create-agent: Creates a new pydantic-ai agent for the Ardoq AI backend. Use when the user wants to add a new agent, build a new chat capability, or asks "create an agent for X".
- create-api: Creates a new API client function for calling ardoq-api endpoints. Use when adding backend integration, wrapping a Clojure endpoint, or when user asks "create an API for X".
- create-postmortem: Writes a post-mortem markdown file under docs/post-mortems/ and publishes it to Confluence (AIP space, "Post Mortems" parent). Use when the user wants to document an incident, write a post-mortem, or RCA.
- create-tool: Creates a new tool function for AI agents. Use when the user wants to add a tool, create a data fetching function, or asks "create a tool for X".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

from ardoq_ai.api.ontology.api import ontology_get
from ardoq_ai.tools.ardoq_tool.tool_decorator import ardoq_tool
from ardoq_ai.tools.features import ArdoqFeature
from ardoq_ai.tools.ontology.schema import OntologyGetOutput


@ardoq_tool(features=[ArdoqFeature.ONTOLOGY])
async def get_ontology(
    model: str | None = None,
) -> OntologyGetOutput:
    """Fetch the OWL ontology for the organisation in DLe (Description Logic expression) syntax.

    The ontology is a formal, machine-readable description of the organisation's metamodel:
    the component types, reference types, fields, and their relationships, expressed as OWL
    classes and properties. It gives a complete structural picture of what kinds of entities
    exist in the Ardoq model and how they relate to one another.

    Use this tool when you need to understand the organisation's metamodel at a structural
    level — for example, to interpret component type names, discover what field types and
    enumerations exist, or reason about how entity types relate.  Prefer the metamodel tools
    (e.g. get_metamodel_fields) when you only need field definitions or type lists, since they
    return lighter, more targeted data.

    Args:
        model: Optional model ID to restrict the ontology to a single metamodel.
            Useful when the organisation has multiple models and you only need the
            schema for one of them.  When omitted, the full org-level ontology is
            returned, covering all models.

    Returns:
        ontology: The OWL ontology as a DLe string, with blank lines removed for
            compactness.  Declares all component types as OWL classes, all reference
            types as object properties, and all fields as data properties, together
            with their domain, range, and any enumeration constraints.
    """
    result = await ontology_get(model=model)
    return OntologyGetOutput(ontology=result)

import onto_helper as oh
import os
import random
import requests


ARDOQ_HOST = "http://ardoqbundlesproduction.localhost:8080"

    "Authorization": f"Token token={API_TOKEN}",
    "Accept": "application/json",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}


# Ardoq API call
# Assuming the headers are all generally similar
def get_entities(endpoint, header=HEADER):
    session = requests.Session()
    session.headers.update(header)

    resp = session.get(endpoint)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()


def compile_entity_type(
    entity_name,
    prefix=None,
    individuals=False,
    endpoint=None,
    output_file=None,
):
    print(f"Get {entity_name}s\n")
    api_endpoint = f"{ARDOQ_HOST}/api/{entity_name}" if not endpoint else endpoint
    entities = get_entities(api_endpoint)

    base_IRI = f"ardoq.{entity_name}s"
    args = {
        "base_IRI": base_IRI,
        "output_file": f"{entity_name}s.ttl" if output_file is None else output_file,
        "data": entities,
        "prefix": prefix,
        "set_binding": prefix is None,
        "ns": base_IRI,
        "individuals": individuals,
        "individual_class": None,
        "key_id": "_id",
        "secondary_id": "id",
    }

    return owl_compiler.compile(args)


def get_metamodel_id(ws_id):
    endpoint = f"{ARDOQ_HOST}/api/workspace/{ws_id}"
    workspace = get_entities(endpoint)
    return workspace["componentModel"]


def get_onto_by_ws_id(ws_id):
    print(f"WORKSPACE: {ws_id}")

    output_folder = ws_id[:8]

    os.makedirs(output_folder, exist_ok=True)

    # WORKSPACE: GET /api/workspace/<ws_id>
    endpoint = f"{ARDOQ_HOST}/api/workspace/{ws_id}"
    compile_entity_type(
        "workspace",
        "ws",
        True,
        endpoint=endpoint,
        output_file=f"{output_folder}/workspace.ttl",
    )

    # - Model: GET /api/model/<mm_id> (defines component + reference types)
    mm_id = get_metamodel_id(ws_id)
    endpoint = f"{ARDOQ_HOST}/api/model/{mm_id}"
    compile_entity_type(
        "metamodel",
        "mm",
        endpoint=endpoint,
        output_file=f"{output_folder}/metamodel.ttl",
    )

    # - Components: GET /api/v2/components?rootWorkspace=<ws_id>
    endpoint = f"{ARDOQ_HOST}/api/v2/components?rootWorkspace={ws_id}"
    compile_entity_type(
        "component",
        "comp",
        True,
        endpoint=endpoint,
        output_file=f"{output_folder}/components.ttl",
    )

    # - References: GET /api/v2/references?rootWorkspace=<ws_id>
    endpoint = f"{ARDOQ_HOST}/api/v2/references?rootWorkspace={ws_id}"
    compile_entity_type(
        "reference",
        "ref",
        True,
        endpoint=endpoint,
        output_file=f"{output_folder}/references.ttl",
    )

    # Combine all
    transform_onto.combine(input_folder=output_folder)


def main():
    endpoint = f"{ARDOQ_HOST}/api/workspace"
    workspaces = get_entities(endpoint)
    ws_ids = [ws["_id"] for ws in workspaces]

    TEST_WS_ID = random.choice(ws_ids)
    get_onto_by_ws_id(TEST_WS_ID)

    # This applies the pellet reasoner to the ontologies
    working_folder = TEST_WS_ID[:8]
    onto, bindings = oh.get_owlready_onto(working_folder, "combined.ttl")
    oh.apply_reasoner(onto)
    oh.save_to_file(onto, bindings, f"{working_folder}/reasoned.ttl")

    # oh.get_ontology_diff(f"{working_folder}/combined.ttl", f"{working_folder}/reasoned.ttl")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

## 1. Ontology Extractor ✅ — main にマージ済み

これがリストの「Ontology API 経由で Ardoq メタモデルを読む」部分。

| 場所 | 内容 |
|---|---|
| `libs/ardoq_ai/ardoq_ai/api/ontology/api.py` | `ontology_get()` — `api/ai-tools/ontology` を呼び、`data["document"]` (DLe文字列) を返す |
| `libs/ardoq_ai/ardoq_ai/tools/ontology/functions.py` | `get_ontology` ツール、`@ardoq_tool(features=[ArdoqFeature.ONTOLOGY])` |
| `libs/ardoq_ai/ardoq_ai/tools/ontology/schema.py` | `OntologyGetOutput` |
| `tools/features.py:14` | フィーチャーフラグ `ONTOLOGY = "ai_internal_ontology"` |
| `agents/ardoq_assistant/agent.py:72` | ardoq_assistant のツールとして登録済み |

マージコミット: `bc428a3a6 AI-1420 Add ontology API client (#1154)`。

サーバー側（DLe生成の実体）は devops-monorepo ではなく **ardoq-api**: `src/ardoq/ai_tools/ontology.clj`, `ontology_api.clj`, `ontology/ont_base.clj`, `ontology/ardoq_owl.clj`。

### 未マージの続き: base ontology ツール
`origin/ontology-base-tools`（main より12コミット先、最終 2026-06-24 Paula Gearon。`origin/ontology-base-tools-ai3` は internal-env-ai-3 向けの同内容）に `list_base_ontologies` / `get_base_ontology` と静的ファイル `libs/ardoq_ai/ardoq_ai/data/ontology/{foundation,application-integration-management,metameta}.dle` がある。**main には存在しない**（`base_ontolog` の grep がゼロ件）。なお当時の署名は `RunContext[BaseContext]` ベースなので、現在の main（context var 方式）に持ってくるには書き換えが必要。

## 2. Ontology Generator — コードは `origin/ontology_generator` ブランチのみ、ただし内容は「文書からの Curator/Ontologist ループ」ではない

`origin/ontology_generator`（main より13コミット先、最終 `73437a6db apply pellet`、2026-07-09 Edvard.lomo、未マージ）:

- `projects/onto_generator/generate_ontology.py` — ワークスペースを選び、`/api/workspace`, `/api/model/<mm_id>`, `/api/v2/components`, `/api/v2/references` を取得して各々 TTL にコンパイル → 結合 → **Pellet reasoner** を適用して `reasoned.ttl` を出力
- `projects/onto_generator/owl_compiler.py` (212行) — JSON→OWL/TTL コンパイラ
- `projects/onto_generator/transform_onto.py` (173行) — 複数 TTL の結合、reference を property 化
- `projects/onto_generator/onto_helper.py` (173行) — owlready2 ラッパー、reasoner、オントロジー差分

つまりこれは **Ardoq のライブデータから OWL を生成するスクリプト群**（LLM なし、`API_TOKEN` + localhost 直叩き、テストなし、moon 統合なし）。あなたが挙げた説明の「Curator/Ontologist loop over documentation」に相当するエージェント実装は、**このリポジトリのどのブランチにも存在しない**（全397 ref に対する `ontologist|curator` の grep がゼロ件）。

## 3. Data Quality Analyzer / Query Generator / Report Generator / EA Modeling Analyzer — このリポジトリには無い

全ブランチ横断 grep（`data_quality`, `quality_analy`, `query_generator`, `generate_query`, `EA Model`）すべてゼロ件。md ドキュメントで `ontolog` / `Extractor` / `Analyzer` に触れるものもゼロ件 — つまりあなたが引用したステータス表そのものも repo 内には無い（Confluence等の外部だと思われる）。

隣の `graphlake` リポジトリも確認したが、`web/ontology_builder.go` と `agent/` があるだけで、これら4機能の名前は一件もヒットしない。

名前が近い既存物（ただし別系統）:
- `libs/ardoq_ai/ardoq_ai/agents/ai_query_builder/` — Query Generator ではなく Ardoq の検索クエリ（gremlin/rule）生成エージェント。main にあり稼働中
- `libs/ardoq_ai/ardoq_ai/agents/entity_extraction/` + `pipeline/implementations/entity_extraction/` — `internal-env-interns` ブランチにある文書からのエンティティ抽出パイプライン（Ontology Extractor とは別物）
- `libs/custom-agents/specs/contract-extraction-agent.json`

## まとめ

6項目のうち、このリポジトリで実際に見つかるのは1.5個です。Ontology Extractor は main に完成・稼働（+ base ontology 拡張が未マージブランチに待機）。Ontology Generator はスクリプト POC が未マージブランチに1つあるだけで、記載されている Curator/Ontologist 型の実装ではありません。残り4項目（Data Quality Analyzer, Query Generator, Report Generator, EA Modeling Analyzer）は、"Partially complete" とされている2つを含め、コードもプロンプトも生成出力も一切見つかりませんでした — 別リポジトリか、コミットされていないローカル作業のどちらかです。
